articles.title: People who are more considerate of others show less “me first” bias in quick decisions
articles.summary: People usually recognize their own belongings faster than someone else’s, even when the items are just pens and pencils. A study found this self-bias was weaker among people who were more attentive to others’ needs and choices.

articles.title: People with darker personalities tend to prefer partners like themselves, study suggests
articles.summary: Why are some people drawn to manipulative or even violent partners? In a study of 400 Brazilian adults, those with darker personality traits tended to rate similar traits as more desirable in a romantic partner.

articles.title: Your body’s state may shape whether your best ideas are verbal or visual
articles.summary: Not all creativity may draw on the same bodily state. In a study that tracked students’ hearts for five days, calmer physiological states went with more original drawings but less original verbal ideas.

articles.summary: Machine learning analysis reveals that different sensory experiences in autistic children correspond to unique patterns of brain connectivity. The research highlights how distinct brain networks shape the way individuals perceive and interact with the physical world.

articles.summary: When danger is real and constant, fictional frights may lose their protective edge. Among Lebanese students facing war and economic crisis, horror fandom was unrelated to resilience.

articles.title: Women’s attention to beauty isn’t limited to the sex they’re attracted to, eye-tracking study finds
articles.summary: When viewing pairs of faces, men linger selectively on attractive faces matching their sexual orientation, while women look longer at attractive faces of either sex, according to new eye-tracking research in Evolution and Human Behavior.

articles.title: Researchers identify female-specific and male-specific genetic risks for anxiety
articles.summary: A massive genetic analysis reveals that while men and women share much of the underlying risk for anxiety, they also possess distinct genetic pathways. These biological differences may explain why anxiety symptoms and prevalence differ by sex.

articles.title: Just 3,000 steps a day may help slow Alzheimer's, scientists find
articles.summary: Walking just 3,000 steps a day could help slow Alzheimer’s-related brain changes, according to new research. Scientists discovered that physical activity was linked to less buildup of harmful tau proteins and nearly half the cognitive and functional decline, even in people already showing early signs of the disease. The strongest benefits appeared at 5,000 to 7,500 daily steps, suggesting that the popular 10,000-step goal may not be necessary.

articles.title: Why some people escape Alzheimer’s despite carrying a high-risk gene
articles.summary: Scientists have discovered why some people with a high genetic risk of Alzheimer’s remain mentally sharp into their 80s, uncovering a rare mutation that protects the brain from harmful protein buildup. The findings reveal a potential new way to prevent early brain damage and could pave the way for treatments that mimic this natural defense.

articles.title: Scientists win 2026 Nobel Prize for controlling brain cells with light
articles.summary: A discovery in tiny algae led to a Nobel Prize-winning breakthrough that allows scientists to switch brain cells on and off using light. The revolutionary technique has already helped researchers activate memories and is opening new possibilities for restoring vision and treating brain disorders.

articles.title: "Mind-blowing" Alzheimer’s breakthrough: Two hours of sleep restored without clearing brain plaques
articles.summary: Scientists have uncovered an unexpected culprit behind sleep loss in Alzheimer’s disease: overactive immune cells in the brain. By temporarily removing these cells, researchers restored more than two hours of sleep per day in mice, revealing a promising new target for treatment.

articles.title: Trust but Verify: Designing Region-Inhomogeneous Forward Dynamics for Discrete Diffusion
articles.summary: arXiv:2610.22380v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Continuous diffusion treats the forward process as a design space; discrete language diffusion often uses absorbing corruption, leaving context fully trusted throughout generation. This makes trust binary: corrupted context is copied as ground truth, propagating errors into generated spans. We reopen this design space by combining absorbing and uniform-mixing kernels with region-dependent rates. articles.title: CGDT-CESN: Correlation-Guided and Dynamics-Trained Clustered Echo State Network for Multivariate Time-Series Prediction
articles.summary: arXiv:2610.22430v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Accurate prediction of multivariate time series requires models that simultaneously capture variable-specific dynamics and cross-variable interactions. In this work, a Correlation-Guided and Dynamics-Trained Clustered Echo State Network (CGDT-CESN) is proposed, which comprises a modular reservoir architecture with each cluster distinctly specializing in one of the variables in the multivariate time series. An innovative reservoir design is proposed in which inter-cluster connections are enabled by empirically observed correlations among variables

articles.summary: arXiv:2610.23231v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Measures of signal complexity have become increasingly popular in electroencephalography (EEG), where they are often interpreted as indicators of neural information processing, dynamical richness, or conscious state.
